newsitem.title: USA: Texaco Inc says agrees settlement terms. [CORRECTED 10:25 GMT 16/11]
newsitem.headline: Texaco Inc says agrees settlement terms. [CORRECTED 10:25 GMT 16/11]

text.p: Texaco Inc confirmed Friday that it has reached a settlement with plaintiffs in a race bias case and agreed to make a one-time payment of $115 million (corrects to insert "million") plus an 11 percent pay increase.
The 1,400 African-American employees who first brought the case in 1994 charge that Texaco systematically discriminated against blacks.
Texaco said that as well as the monetary compensation and salary increase the company will set up four programs designed to ensure fairness.

The company said in a statement that it agreed to set up an Equality and Tolerance Task Force which will be charged with determining potential improvements to Texaco's human resources programs, as well as helping to monitor the progress in those programs, with three members being appointed by the plaintiffs and three by Texaco and a mutually agreed chairman.
Texaco will also adopt and implement company-wide diversity and sensitivity monitoring and ombuds programs.
It will consider nationwide job posting of more senior positions than are currently posted. Also, it will monitor its performance on the programs and initiatives provided for under the settlement.

Texaco's chairman and chief executive, Peter Bijur, said in the statement: "With this litigation behind us, we can now move forward on our broader, urgent mission to make Texaco a model of workplace opportunity for all men and women."

"Texaco is committed to developing and instituting specific, effective policies that will ensure that discrimination is wiped out wherever it may be, and that will expand the positive economic impact clearly defined and achievable - with measurable goals set out on a specific timetable," he added.

"Today's agreement affords us a renewed opportunity to join in common purpose and unified action to achieve shared goals of greater inclusion and opportunity at Texaco - and in America," Bijur concluded.
